On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape Udayaditya is the forceful liberator and Sitaram the submissive guard. Udayaditya comes sword in hand to the locked door, kicks it and orders it opened. Sitaram opens at once but with folded hands pleads orders that no one leave the inner quarters. When Udayaditya draws his sword and asks if he will take up arms against him, Sitaram with folded hands refuses, saying Udayaditya has twice saved his life, takes the dust of his feet, and begs Udayaditya to save that life a third time by disarming him, taking his weapon, and binding him head to foot so the Maharaj will spare him tomorrow. Udayaditya ties him up with his own cloth, leaves him lying there, and goes out.

On the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison the positions are reversed. Sitaram throws open the prison door, enters the dark room, announces himself, and tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire and to come out quickly. Where Udayaditya had demanded and threatened, now it is Udayaditya who asks "Who is it?" and "Why?" Sitaram grabs him and almost carries him out. After long confinement, Udayaditya stands helpless in the open field asking what he should do and where he should go, and it is Sitaram who leads him away.

Pratapaditya first orders two Pathan brothers to kill Basanta Ray on his way to Jessore when he shelters at the inn in Simultali — one to lure his retainers away with a false alarm of dacoits attacking a village, leaving him alone on a deserted road at night for the other to murder. The assigned killer spares him after passing the night listening to his sitar and talk, and confesses the plot. Later Pratapaditya sends Muktiyar Khan with a signed death sentence and soldiers to Raigarh, who capture Udayaditya in the field, enter the fort in plain clothes during evening prayers, show Basanta Ray the written order, and on Muktiyar's call Abdul enters with a drawn sword and kills him.

In the Jessore palace inner quarters while disguised as a middle-aged woman, Rammohan lifts him into the air, swings him around, ties him in a shawl and carries him out over his shoulder; in the king's room in the Chandradwip palace appearing as himself the jester, Rammohan grabs him by the scruff of the neck and throws him out of the room.
The Rajmahishi secretly sends for love-winning medicine from Mangala, who instead spends five days preparing poison to kill Surma so the Yubaraj will feel no pity when she dies.

Her refusal leads her husband Ramchandra Ray to take another wife, so when she finally comes to Chandradwip she finds the Maharaj getting married and has no place or home left in her own kingdom and royal palace.

Rukmini visits Udayaditya on a stormy night while he is alone holding a sleeping girl, plays on his guilt for having ruined her, and when he offers to give her whatever she wants she asks for the ring on his finger. He pulls it off and throws it down, and she takes it.

That ring bears Udayaditya's name-seal. Sitaram and Bhagavat, who are secretly conferring with Rukmini, use it to forge a petition in Udayaditya's name to the Emperor accusing Pratapaditya of treason in order to take the kingdom, and stamp it with the seal.

Bhagavat then carries the forged petition not to Delhi but to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya was taking it to Delhi, the servant fled, and he recovered it. After reading it Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya to be imprisoned.

Udayaditya's forcing of the locked doors to get Ramchandra out left the two guards who had been overpowered and bound — Sitaram and Bhagavat — to face Pratapaditya's punishment, and they were dismissed. Feeling guilty because they suffered for letting him pass, Udayaditya fixed a monthly stipend for them. Pratapaditya, who was now watching Udayaditya closely, took this mercy as defiance and forbade any further help. Udayaditya and Surma then had Surma send the money secretly to their families through a trusted maid, who told Mangala, and word reached Pratapaditya. Unable to force Surma directly, he retaliated for the disobeyed prohibition by ordering that Surma be sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray's grief at surviving into emptiness — that those he sang for, laughed with, and longed to embrace no longer answer his call, so song comes on its own but without joy, like a man left as the sole broken remnant with only himself to live on.

He sings it first on the veranda of his palace in Raigarh in the afternoon, gazing at the setting sun beyond the field and mango grove without his sitar, in wistful, spontaneous remembrance; when questioned he repeats its burden about what remains being only emptiness and illusion, saying his sitar's strings are broken and cannot be tuned, yet he can still be swept into vigorous, clapping, joyful singing together with Khan Saheb.

He sings it second in Jessore in the inner quarters, after rushing there on news of Udayaditya's imprisonment and finding Surma's once-joyful room silent, dark and utterly empty. Standing before the door with Vibha alone beside him like the last remnant of a happy family, taking her hand, he slowly sings the same line as a realized lament — no longer nostalgic musing but desolate wail that those who were there are here no more.

Rukmini tries to tear Udayaditya away at the boat but is pulled off Sitaram, throws herself into the monsoon-swollen canal, and survives. Returning from the water she vows revenge, goes before Pratapaditya, tells him the Yubaraj escaped in the night with the old king of Raigarh through Sitaram's plot with fire and false death, and demands men to hunt them herself. With her guidance Pratapaditya's men verify Udayaditya is in Raigarh, and on that intelligence he sends Muktiyar Khan on a secret order. Rukmini stays in Raigarh and herself finds Udayaditya alone in the field at dusk, calls the torch-bearing soldiers to surround and detain him, and while he is held helpless Muktiyar Khan steals into the fort in plain clothes and beheads Basanta Ray at his evening prayer.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra with cold, deliberate indifference. No festive welcome is prepared — no lighting of the path, no musical fanfare, only a late, small escort with a small elephant. When they meet, Pratapaditya remains seated with his minister, offers only a calm “Come. Are you well?”, then turns to state business, reads a long document on a tax complaint, briefly asks about floods, interrupts his son-in-law to return to reading, and finally dismisses him to the inner quarters.

Ramchandra later inverts this in his own court through active, vindictive ridicule. Presiding from his throne, he encourages daily attacks on Pratapaditya’s status: his lineage is mocked as only two generations old, as earthworm to leech to hooded snake, his father is said to have begged Ramchandra’s grandfather for anointment with the toe of his left foot, and his house is said to be redeemed for seven generations merely by the marriage. Ramchandra listens smiling, smoking his hookah and laughing, allowing minister, dewan and jester to tear Pratapaditya and Udayaditya to shreds. Where Pratapaditya asserted superiority by ignoring his son-in-law, Ramchandra asserts it by degrading his father-in-law before flatterers.

The older lone widow Udayaditya confesses to having fallen for at eighteen in Raigarh is Rukmini. She leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore, supporting herself by money-lending and keeping many under her control through beauty and silver. Sensual, envious and greedy for dominion, she hopes that when the Yubaraj ascends the throne she will rule his heart and Jessore together. She befriends all the palace servants, tracks every trivial news from the palace, and performs vows, tantric rituals and death-rites for Pratapaditya and Surma.

When the King and Queen's animosity toward Surma grows to a proposal to send her away, the Queen hears that the widow Mangala knows tantra, mantra and medicine and, with the King's consent, sends Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from her to win the Yubaraj's heart back from Surma. Mangala spends a whole night cutting, soaking, grinding, mixing roots and chanting mantras, taking five days to prepare a poison with rituals so that the Yubaraj will feel no pity when Surma dies. On the eve of Surma's departure she suffers strange distress, cold limbs and failing breath in Udayaditya's arms, and dies with four dandas of night remaining, the death spreading through the palace as suicide by poison she took herself.

Later, on a stormy night, Rukmini herself enters Udayaditya's dark bolted bedchamber with a lamp while he sits holding a sleeping child Surma had loved, reproaches him for ruining her and leaving her to wander like a beggar, demands his love and a place at his window on his chest, tries to sit on his bed, and takes the ring from his finger.

In the beginning Udayaditya tells Surma he wishes he had never been born in a royal palace as the crown prince and sole heir to wealth, honor and glory. He feels he was born only as an heir, not as a son — his father watches him with an examiner's eye to see if he can uphold earned fame and bear the kingdom's burden, while relatives, ministers and subjects scrutinize him and judge him a fool incapable of protecting the perilous kingdom. He internalizes this, saying he truly has no intellect for rule: at sixteen, given charge of the Hosenkhali pargana, within six months revenue fell, disorder arose, and the court concluded that because he was beloved by subjects he could never rule, after which his father despised him as a disgrace who, like his uncle Basanta Ray of Raigarh, would play sitar and ruin the kingdom.

Later, brought as a prisoner before Pratapaditya, he is taken alone into a room. Asked what punishment fits him, he answers, whatever you command. Told he is not worthy of the kingdom, he assents, says he does not want the kingdom, and begs release from the throne to leave for Kashi, asking only for money to build a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name. When asked for proof of sincerity, he offers to touch the feet of Ma-Kali and swear he will never rule even a needle's tip of land and that Samaraditya shall be heir. Pratapaditya agrees, and that very day in the temple before him Udayaditya swears with Ma-Kali as witness that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of the Maharaja of Jessore's kingdom, will not sit on the throne, will not touch the royal scepter, and if he ever does, may the sin of his grand-uncle's murder be his.

Nayanchand, fearing Pratapaditya's wrath, delivers Ramchandra Ray's letter renouncing Vibha to the Mahishi instead of to Pratapaditya. The Mahishi hides it from both Pratapaditya and Vibha, confides it only to Basanta Ray, and on his advice announces throughout the household that Ramchandra has written requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal adjoining the palace blocked immediately with large Sal wood logs to trap Ramchandra Ray's boat in it and ordered no one be allowed to leave the inner quarters that night. During the escape the boat went a short distance and was stopped by the logs, but Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs. The guards suddenly saw the boat escaping from afar and threw stones, but not one reached. They had swords but no guns; one went to fetch a gun, and after frantic search a gun was found but no flintlock, gunpowder or bullets could be found. The guards then sent for a boat to give chase, but the man sent stopped on the way to smoke tobacco and press for a debt, the chase boat arrived long after it was needed, and the guards wasted three times longer berating him than the delay itself, so there was no longer any chance of catching the boat before it reached the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray's sitar was his eternal companion and voice of joy, but as he is torn from Udayaditya it becomes a measure of his despair. At parting he plays furiously through blurring tears until his throat chokes and he must put it down, then leaves it behind declaring he will not play anymore. Later, alone, he can only hum to himself, and when asked where it is he says it is there but its strings have broken and can no longer be tuned — an image of his own broken heart. His songs turn to emptiness and being left alone behind, showing that without Udayaditya there is no one left to sing for and no joy left in music.

Previously he was known for going out whenever he pleased, involving himself in the affairs of the subjects even against his father's wishes, treating danger as a trifle and fighting oppression with all his might, stopping an official without considering the consequences to protect a subject.

Afterwards his former courage was gone and a blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of him, leaving hesitation and doubt in every task. When he heard of a plan to send men at night to loot and burn the estate office of the zamindar of Chhapra he ordered his horse readied and then sent it away; when he saw a royal official beating a subject tied to a tree who cried to him for mercy he ran into his house instead of intervening; and when the stipends for Bhagavat and Sitaram were stopped he no longer had the courage to help them with money openly or secretly, resolving to send it but always hesitating until it was never sent.
He frees Udayaditya from the imprisonment caused by the forged petition by using a fire to draw the guards away and carrying him out of his prison cell to open ground.

On one occasion he carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down from the palace roof to the boat waiting in the canal about seventy cubits below, climbing down a huge rope made by twisting together thick sheets tied to a small pillar that ends a little above the boat, then gripping the rope with his teeth at the end to free both hands to release the king from his back and lower him carefully into the boat before jumping down himself.

On the other occasion, after Vibha is insulted, rejected and faints to the floor, he lifts her unconscious body in his arms, carries her out of the palace to the palanquins by the gate, lays her in one of them and takes her back to the boat.

In Jessore she is dressed as an over-adorned royal bride for her husband's arrival, against her own taste: eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet forced on each fair, delicate arm instead of the three thin turquoise bangles she wanted, a large nose ring forced on her small delicate face, and a heavy coiffure imposed by her mother after her own preferred styling is undone — leaving her burdened with jewelry and hair, shy and flustered but full of joy.

In Chandradwip she strips herself of every royal marker to seek him out: dressed as a common woman, refusing a palanquin because she is no queen, insisting on going on foot like a subject and a beggar-woman with only a veil over her head, entering the palace unrecognized like a maidservant with no welcome, falling at his feet in tears until the king himself mistakes her for a beggar woman come seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death the window is a place of absence and remembered presence. He leaves empty the spot where Surma used to sit, sits beside it looking out at the unchanged moonlight, garden and breeze, and clings to the impossible hope that opening the door he will still find her sitting there.

In the prison cell the window becomes a place of freedom and future life. The small opening with its sliver of sky, birds in flight, bamboo grove and temple lets him remember that his cage will one day break, that he will swim in the endless sky. The two hands' breadth of ground by the window is where he feels naturally free beyond any king's captivity, while the soft bed inside the room has become the true prison.

It begins as a flirtatious borrowing arrangement. The widowed Rukmini lives by lending cash at interest and holding men by beauty and money, and the penniless but stylish palace guard Sitaram is drawn to both. He strolls to her house when he has no food, begs in rhyming jest for gold and silver not favor, invents that his mother who keeps his money has gone to Joraghata and he will repay tomorrow, and she laughs and gives it as if not thrown in water with no hope of return.

Emboldened, he overflows with love-play, calls her his Subhadra to his Jagannath, argues foolishly that if Subhadra were sister there could be no Subhadraharan, melts when she calls him fool, and at her prompting repeats after her Pran, Priye, Priyatame, Pranpriye. When he asks what interest she will charge she pouts that this is not love, and he passes it off as a joke. Repayment is then forgotten, visits become frequent and secret, with talk of a scheme needing Bhagavat's help.

The break comes with the Yubaraj's imprisonment. Sitaram rushes to her hut, curses her as ruinous, all but strikes her, and threatens to set her house on fire, grind her face on stone, smear it with lime and soot without drinking water, and drive her from the city after he returns from Raigarh. She listens with clenched teeth, tightened fists, trembling limbs and hate gathering in her eyes as if a curse will fall on him, then claims the Yubaraj is hers alone to save or harm and dares him to free him.

It turns life-threatening after Sitaram's arson to fake the Yubaraj's death in prison. Needing to flee Jessore, he stops to loot her, thinking her dead and heirless. He finds the door open and her sitting sleepless, trembling, in a wet cloth with dripping hair and ashen face in lamplight like a ghost returned from Yama's door. She vows to lay him and the Yubaraj in an oven and smear herself with their pyre-ash before she dies. He tries to revert to soft affection and singing, which only enrages her more until she hunts for a curved blade to make him pay, strikes repeatedly at the floor where he stood after he slips out, and he flees that night with his family thinking he should have strangled her because she knows of the escape.

Sitaram first uses fire as a distraction to clear the guards. Huts in the long row where the guards live near the prison are set alight in several places at once in the evening, and the guards at Udayaditya's door — who keep only a customary watch because he sits so quietly and seems to have no desire to escape — are the first to run to save their own cots, utensils, clothes and belongings.

The distraction is then deliberately prolonged. The simultaneous outbreak in five or six rooms is not accident, and Sitaram's men among the commoners, palace servants and even among the fire-fighters keep it from going out — pouring water where there is no fire, going to fetch water and not bringing it back, breaking water pots, stumbling into one another and creating confusion, while crowds gathering to watch further hinder the work.

Under cover of that chaos, while everyone is occupied at the guardhouse, Sitaram's men set the now-empty prison cell itself on fire — windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, wooden fences — a place no one would expect to burn and so no one watches. Sitaram, after seeing Udayaditya off by boat and taking his sword from him, throws bones, a skull and the sword into the burning cell.

He then stages discovery: shouts that the Yubaraj's cell has caught fire, planted voices claiming the Yubaraj was seen through the window and heard screaming inside, and Sitaram himself running up crying that the roof has collapsed and there is no response from him. When the guards run over they find the building collapsed and fire everywhere with no way to enter, and fall to blaming and cursing one another.

In this way the escape is converted into an apparent death — with witnesses, screams, an unenterable burnt cell, and the melted burnt remains of the sword produced as relics — allowing Sitaram to spread the news that the Yubaraj has died in the fire and remain untroubled for some time.

He feels no gratitude and treats the rescue as something that was bound to happen, believing that if he were in peril the whole world would naturally unite to save him. He convinces himself Udayaditya saved him not for his sake but for his sister Vibha's sake, and dismisses the act entirely for the crime of Udayaditya being Pratapaditya's son. Even to the extent he feels thanks, he joins the minister and Ramai Bhand in laughing at and tearing Udayaditya to shreds, lacking the mental strength to silence the mockery or refrain from joining in.

Pratapaditya dismisses the minister's warning that killing Basanta Ray will displease the Emperor of Delhi, declares the Emperor is not his God, calls fear of him deeply insulting, and forbids the minister to speak his name until the murder is done, boasting that he himself will judge and punish the Emperor.

Bhagavat and Sitaram then turn that dismissed authority into a weapon against Prince Udayaditya by forging a petition as if the Yubaraj were lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor to win the kingdom for himself, stamping it with the Yubaraj's name using the seal-ring Rukmini had brought. Bhagavat carries it not to Delhi but to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted a servant of Udayaditya taking it toward Delhi, which makes Pratapaditya believe his son has appealed to the Delhi power to betray him and provides the pretext to imprison him.

Vibha's hair is dressed to her own taste only by Surma. When her mother imposes heavy adornment and an unbearable hairstyle, Vibha secretly has Surma redo it to her liking, which her mother undoes again while accusing Surma of ruining it from jealousy. After Surma is gone, at braiding time Vibha sits quietly waiting as if Surma will come to braid it, and evening falls into night with her hair still unbraided. Her hair then remains unkempt, with a sorrowful face and no smile, the visible mark that there is no one left to care for her.
